chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: New session, April 27: the list of bandleaders he arranged for
summary: Horace reads his list: Barnet, Jimmy Dorsey, Lunceford, Tiny Hill, Ralph Marterie, Ben Pollack, Goodman, Phil Spitalny's violinist idea, Claude Hopkins, Millinder, Hal McIntyre, Duke Dailey, Basie and Earl Hines.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: (Reel 12.)

This is Sunday, April 27th, 1975, and we're once again with Horace Henderson in our -- must be fourth or fifth interview. Can't remember just where we are. Anyhow, Horace, I think we talked previously about the possibility of your discussing the various persons for whom you have arranged and also tried to dig into somewhat of the arranging scene itself as to sort of styles and what you were doing when, with whom, et cetera.

You've prepared a list there of the various bands and band leaders for whom you have done arranging through the years. Why don't you just make a record of this? Why don't you read the list, and then we can go from there?
All right, Tom. I should say, how are you today.
I'm fine, man. You're a busy man, you know. (Laughter and inaudible remarks)
Well, I tell you, getting right down to it, I wrote down a few great band leaders here that I had the privilege of writing a little bit for and, well, number one
was Charlie Barnet and that great band that he had.
This was when? Late '30's or --
This was in the late '30's, I would say. Yes. And, of course, the late Jimmy Dorsey and the late Jimmy Lunceford at that Margie deal (unintelligible), you know?
Oh, yeah. Right.
That was Jimmy Henderson, did arrange "Margie," but . . . He was --
That was a popular --
Yeah, he was -- that was quite a hit, and he had that little Snooky Young trumpet player. I think he's with the NBC band right now.
Is he really?

Yes. Now another guy I had the privilege of arranging for, and it was quite a challenge, because it was a different style and everything. We'll get into that later, but we'll put down the big, heavy bandleader at that time, Tiny Hill.
Oh, yes.
He played quite a bit of corn --
Tiny Hill lived here in Denver for some time or at Fort Lupton.
Yes, Fort Lupton, Colorado, yes, he did. He farmed 100 acres and so forth, and he had a 24 hour radio station. But we'll get back to that, though.
Right.

Then Ralph Marteri and his trumpet, and another guy that just passed recently, Ben Pollock. He had a nightclub in Palm Springs for quite some time. I read about this. This was later on, you know. Then, of course, the great Benny Goodman. And there is another guy that I accepted a position to write a little bit, and it was quite a challenge, because it was an honor that he wanted me to do some writing (Dave-ed) for him, and that was Phil Rubenoff, the great violinist, and that was in New York City, and he wanted a jazz band, all that stuff, you know.

Then, of course, Claude Hopkins, who played the Roseland Ballroom in New York, and the great Lucky Millinder, and I had the pleasure of doing a few things for Hal McIntyre, and a guy that disappeared, and they've never found out about him, and he had a great band in New York. Do you remember a bandleader named Duke Dailey?
No, I don't think I do.

He was quite a character, and -- but he loved to fly planes. This was the very end. We haven't heard of him since. And, of course, the great Count Basie. And one of my idols, Earl Hines. So there are more, but this is a few that I have written down. So --
That's great. May I have the list?
Sure.
